wstep: This card describes how to dry whole black currants in a dehydrator or oven at 140 °F (60 °C), after cracking the skins in boiling water.

akapity: CSU describes black currants together with grapes; this card does not cover red currants.
Wash and sort the currants and remove the stems; dry them whole.
Discard any fruit that shows decay, bruises or mould: such defects can affect all of the dried product.
Currants have tough skins with a wax-like coating: before drying them whole, crack the skins so that inside moisture can evaporate.
Dip the currants in boiling water for 30 seconds to crack the skins, then in very cold water.
Drain the fruit on absorbent towels before placing it on the trays.
Dry the fruit at 140 °F (60 °C) in a dehydrator or oven.
Do not use trays or screens made of galvanized mesh; also avoid copper and aluminium mesh.
Only use an oven if it can be set as low as 140 °F (60 °C); if it cannot go that low, the fruit cooks instead of drying.
In an oven, keep 140–150 °F (about 60–66 °C): place a calibrated oven thermometer on the rack or tray and check it every 2 hours throughout drying.
Leave the oven door open 2–3 inches (about 5–7.5 cm) so moisture can escape.
In a conventional oven, drying can take up to twice as long as in a dehydrator, depending on air circulation.
Fruit scorches easily near the end of drying: when drying is almost done, turn the oven heat off and open the door wide for one more hour.
Dry until the fruit is pliable and leathery with no moist centre; this takes 12–24 hours.
Before testing for dryness, take out a few pieces and let them cool to room temperature: warm fruit seems softer, moister and more pliable than it really is.

The fruit is dry when, after you squeeze a handful, no moisture is left on your hand and the pieces spring apart when released; cut cooled pieces show no visible moisture and none can be squeezed out.
Home dried fruit should contain about 20% moisture.
After drying, cool the fruit for 30–60 minutes before packing; do not wait too long to pack it, because moisture could get back into it.
Pack only completely cooled fruit: warm dried food sweats, and that moisture can be enough for mould to grow.
Condition the cooled fruit: pack it loosely in closed jars for 7–10 days and shake the jars daily.
If condensation develops in a jar, return the fruit to the dehydrator.
Store the dried fruit in clean, dry canning jars, plastic freezer containers with tight-fitting lids or plastic freezer bags.
Packaging must be food grade: do not use trash bags or plastic or fibreboard containers that previously held non-food items.
Pack amounts that can be used at one time: each opening exposes the dried fruit to air and moisture, which lowers quality and can lead to spoilage.
Vacuum packaging is not a preservation method by itself: removing oxygen increases the risk of botulism, and a product that needs refrigeration still needs it.
Store the dried fruit in a cool, dry, dark place.
Most dried fruits can be stored for 1 year at 60 °F (about 16 °C) and 6 months at 80 °F (about 27 °C); the warmer, the shorter.
Check the dried fruit often (glass shows condensation); if it has taken up moisture but is not spoiled, use it at once or dry it again and repack it.
Throw away mouldy dried fruit; also throw away dried fruit that smells off.
